h1: Tasting a strong Indian lager against a pilsner side by side
title: Strong Indian Lager vs Pilsner | Craft Beer School
desc: A side by side tasting of a strong Indian lager and a pilsner: what to pour, what to look for and why the two taste so different.
teaser: Both are pale, cold and fizzy. Taste them together and they turn out to be almost opposite beers.
standfirst: The strong lager is the most familiar beer in India. The pilsner is the style most of the world's lagers descend from. Tasting them next to each other is one of the quickest ways to learn what malt, hops, adjuncts and alcohol each do.
sections: Why this pairing teaches so much

A strong Indian lager and a pilsner look alike in the glass. Both are pale gold and bottom fermented. That is where the similarity ends. One is built for strength and smoothness, the other for crisp bitterness. Put them side by side and every difference you notice points at a choice the brewer made.

We use this pairing with beginners because nobody needs training to notice the contrast. It is a good first step towards tasting with intent.

The strong lager. Usually somewhere between about 6 and 8% ABV. Often brewed with rice, maize or sugar alongside barley malt. Frequently brewed at high gravity and then diluted. Bitterness is low. The aim is a smooth, slightly sweet beer with noticeable alcohol warmth.

The pilsner. Usually around 4.5 to 5.2% ABV, made mostly or entirely with pale malt and hopped generously with spicy, floral European hops. Czech examples are fuller and rounder. German examples are drier and sharper. Our pilsner style guide covers both. An 8% strong lager carries roughly 60% more alcohol than a 5% pilsner. You will taste that.

• Use two identical clear glasses so neither beer gets an advantage.
  • Pour about 100 ml of each. Small pours are enough to taste and keep the session sensible.
  • Serve both at around 5 to 7 °C. Too cold and you will taste nothing.
  • Have water and plain crackers on the side.
  • Taste the pilsner first. The strong lager's alcohol and sweetness linger and can dull your palate for the lighter beer.

If you can, ask a friend to pour so you taste without knowing which is which. You will be surprised how often people change their minds blind.

Hold both against a white page. The strong lager may be a shade deeper. Watch the foam: an all-malt pilsner often holds a denser, longer-lasting head because malt protein supports foam, while beers heavy in rice or sugar have less of it.

Now smell. The pilsner should give you bread, cracker and a spicy, herbal or floral hop note. Some pilsners carry a faint sulphur note that fades as the glass sits. The strong lager tends to smell sweeter: honey, cooked grain, sometimes a hint of corn. A spirity edge appears as it warms.

Sip the pilsner and wait. The bitterness arrives late and dries the palate, which makes you want another sip. That clean, bitter finish is the point of the style.

Sip the strong lager. It feels fuller and softer in the middle, partly from residual sugar and partly from the alcohol itself, which adds body and a little sweetness. The finish is warm rather than bitter. Hop character is faint. If the beer has been sitting in a hot shop, you may also catch a stale, papery note from oxidation.

Note what you like. Neither beer is wrong. They were designed for different jobs.

Every gap you noticed has a cause on the brewhouse floor. Thinner foam points at adjuncts. Sweetness and warmth point at strength and residual sugar. The pilsner's bite points at hops added in quantity during the boil. To understand the adjunct side better, read our guide to rice and maize adjuncts in India.

Once you can link a sensation to a process, tasting stops being a matter of opinion. That link is what trained tasters build over months. It is also the part that is hard to learn from articles alone.
Mistakes that spoil a side by side

Most failed comparisons go wrong in the set-up, not the tasting. Pouring one beer into a mug and the other into a tulip changes how each smells. Serving one straight from the fridge and the other after it has sat on the table makes the warm one seem sweeter and flatter. Tasting a chilli-heavy snack between glasses wipes out bitterness. Keep everything equal except the beer.

Freshness is the other trap. A pilsner that sat in a hot shop for months will have lost its hop aroma and may taste of honey and paper, which makes it seem closer to the strong lager than it really is. Check the packing date on both and buy from a shop that keeps beer in a cooler. If one beer tastes stale, note it and try again with a fresher bottle before drawing conclusions.

Add a third glass. A helles sits between the two: malty and soft like the strong lager but at pilsner strength with no adjuncts. A light lager shows what happens when you push adjuncts further and strength down. Three or four small pours make a proper flight. Keep the pours small, share them and drink water between beers.
faqs: Is strong Indian lager a recognised beer style?
Not in most international style guides, but it is a distinct and very popular category in India: pale, sweetish, low in bitterness and usually between about 6 and 8% ABV.
Why does strong lager taste sweet?
Higher strength brings more residual sugar and the alcohol itself adds a sweet, full impression. Low hop bitterness means nothing balances that sweetness.
Which should I taste first in a side by side?
The pilsner. The strong lager's alcohol and sweetness linger and make the lighter beer seem thin if you taste it second.
Why does pilsner foam last longer?
All-malt beers have more of the proteins that hold foam together. Beers brewed with a lot of rice, maize or sugar usually have a lighter, less stable head.
